newsitem.title: USA: State security regulators okay adviser scheme.
newsitem.headline: State security regulators okay adviser scheme.

text.p: U.S. state and provincial securities regulators approved a new plan that calls for small investment adviser competency exams and heightened consumer awareness, an investment protection group said Monday.

The new initiative, approved Sunday, is geared toward the growing number of consumers who use small investment advisers and financial planners, North American Securities Administrators Association Inc (NASAA) said in a statement.

A Memorandum of Understanding calls for yearly training of new regulatory personnel, sharing information and communication support among provincial and state securities regulators and cooperative operations states to assure adviser compliance with state laws and regulations.
The memo, approved at NASAA's spring conference here, also calls for working groups to develop uniform financial and record keeping regulations for state-registered advisers.
According to the memo, NASAA will develop an exam for its members testing knowledge of subject matter and competency of state-registered investment adviser representatives.

The memo also states NASAA will create a database containing resumes of members with an expertise in adviser examinations, persons willing to serve as expert witnesses and potential "case coordinators".

The plan, stated to become effective in July, is a provision of the National Securities Markets Improvement Act, sweeping securities reform legistation designed to do away with overlapping state and federal regulations of advisers.
The Securities and Exchange Commission retained oversight of investment advisers with more than $25 million in assets under management.
The new plan will give states primary regulatory responsibility for some 19,000 of the 25,000 investment advisers and financial planners nationwide.
"We are committee to having this plan implemented by July 8th when these financial professionals become our exclusive regulatory charge," said NASAA President Mark Griffin.
